aboutAuthor: Ted Seides, co-founder of Protégé Partners and host of the Capital Allocators podcast, interviewed hundreds of elite money managers. This book distills how the world's best investors actually run their firms — and their capital.

points.heading: Capital allocation is the job
points.body: A great investor's core skill isn't picking stocks but deciding where each marginal dollar goes: new bets, bigger bets, or returned to owners. The best allocators treat capital as finite ammunition and deploy it with deliberate asymmetry.

points.heading: Alignment before returns
points.body: Seides shows top managers screen for alignment first: significant personal capital invested alongside clients, reasonable fees, capacity discipline. A manager who eats his own cooking behaves very differently in a drawdown than one who doesn't.

points.heading: Process beats prediction
points.body: Elite allocators build repeatable processes for sourcing, diligence, and sizing decisions rather than relying on brilliance. They write down theses, pre-mortem their mistakes, and grade themselves on decision quality — not just outcomes.

points.heading: Sizing reveals conviction
points.body: The difference between a good idea and a good investment is position size. The managers Seides profiles size positions by conviction and liquidity, cut losers without ego, and let winners compound far longer than comfort suggests.

points.heading: Relationships are alpha
points.body: Access flows through networks: the best deals and the best managers are visible only to people who have earned trust over decades. Seides argues that relationship building is a compounding asset exactly like capital.

points.heading: Know thyself — then hire around it
points.body: Every allocator has blind spots; the great ones institutionalize self-knowledge. They surround themselves with partners whose strengths offset their weaknesses and create cultures where disagreement is safe and expected.

insights: Seides famously took the other side of Warren Buffett's famous S&P 500 versus hedge-funds bet.
Chapters open with anonymized anecdotes drawn from real manager interviews.
The book functions as an unofficial curriculum for aspiring chief investment officers.
conclusion: Capital Allocators reveals that superior investing is organizational: aligned incentives, disciplined process, honest sizing, and trusted relationships. Money follows judgment, and judgment follows character.
